title: E-commerce Payment Setup in Southeast Asia: Building Infrastructure That Scales With Growth
summary: Learn how to build an e-commerce payment setup in Southeast Asia covering local payments through one integration with Xendit. The post E-commerce Payment Setup in Southeast Asia: Building Infrastructure That Scales With Growth appeared first on Xendit .
body_markdown:
An e-commerce payment setup in Southeast Asia is more complex than one built for a single country. Your business has to


**support several markets** at the same time, and each market runs on its own


**mix of preferred payment methods** . Regional growth adds to that, because the number of customers your setup has to serve keeps rising in every one of those markets.


[Southeast Asia's digital economy](https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/e_conomy_sea_2025_report.pdf) is on track to surpass


**USD 300 billion in gross merchandise value** , around 1.5 times the figure Google, Temasek, and Bain forecast in their first e-Conomy report a decade ago, with GMV and revenue both growing at roughly


**15% year over year** . For your business, that growth means more customers to reach across the region, and more checkout sessions where the payment options you offer determine whether an order is completed, since customers in each market expect the payment methods they use.


To reach those customers, your business has to work with different payment behaviors and preferences in every market. A payment checkout that performs well in Singapore will produce a different result in Indonesia or Thailand, because customers in each market reach for local wallets, bank transfers, QR payments, or cards depending on where they shop and what they use regularly.


Your payment setup involves three things at once, which are the


**payment methods** you accept, the


**systems** that process and confirm each transaction, and the


**records** your teams work from once the order is placed. When any of those three fails to match how a customer wants to buy, you lose the order at checkout, where the customer had already decided to buy.


**Here is what this article covers:**


- Where payment friction appears for e-commerce businesses selling across Southeast Asia, from missing methods to sales that happen outside a traditional checkout


- What your payment infrastructure needs to provide as order volume, market count, and sales channels increase


- How MASSHIRO&Co. moved from declining international orders to accepting both foreign cards and local payment methods


- How to build a payment setup that accommodates online checkout, chat-based selling, and eventual offline retail without a separate build for each


## **Where e-commerce payment friction happens across Southeast Asian markets**


Payment friction rarely shows up in your analytics as a payment problem. It appears as cart abandonment, an unfulfilled order, or a support ticket, and the cause usually falls into one of five patterns.


Here are the


**five most common sources of e-commerce payment friction in Southeast Asia** , and what each one costs your business:


### **1. Your checkout is missing the payment method the customers prefer**


**Payment preference differs** at every border in this region. A customer may want to pay with a local e-wallet, a bank transfer, a QR code, or a card that your checkout does not support, and the absence of that one option may end the transaction.


QR has become a particular blind spot.


[Ten countries in Southeast Asia](https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/e_conomy_sea_2025_report.pdf) **now operate national QR systems** with strong adoption, and eight markets offer cross-border QR interoperability. For your business, a checkout built without QR in those markets asks a growing share of customers to fall back on a payment habit they have already moved away from.


***Also read:***[QR Ph Payments in the Philippines: A Business Guide to the Country's National QR Standard](https://www.xendit.co/en-ph/blog/qr-ph-payments-in-the-philippines-a-business-guide-to-the-countrys-national-qr-standard/)


The work is for your business to set the payment method mix market by market, based on what customers in each country already use.


### **2. Customers face different payment experiences in each market**


An e-commerce business operating across the region often ends up with a different checkout in each country, assembled from whichever local provider was available at the time.


Customers notice those differences because payment channels complete in different ways. Some redirect the customer to a bank or e-wallet app to authenticate, others present a payment code or QR for the customer to act on separately, and others need no customer action at all once the payment is initiated.


Your checkout has to handle all three of these


**completion flows** , which are redirect, present a code, and no action required. When it handles one of them poorly, customers meet an unfamiliar or broken step at the moment they are ready to pay.


### **3. Customers may purchase through different sales channels**


A large share of e-commerce demand now starts and finishes outside a product page. Video commerce alone accounts for


[25%](https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/e_conomy_sea_2025_report.pdf) of total e-commerce GMV in the region, and many purchases are agreed directly in chat with a seller on Instagram, WhatsApp, or during a live session.


For your business, sending a customer from a chat thread back to a website to complete payment adds steps at the exact moment they have decided to buy. Your team needs a way to


**collect payment inside the channel** where the conversation is already happening.


***Also read:[How Payment Success Rates Turn Checkout Demand Into E-Commerce Revenue](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/how-payment-success-rates-turn-checkout-demand-into-e-commerce-revenue/)***


### **3. Payment operations get heavier as order volume rises**


More transactions mean more payment statuses, refunds, settlements, and transaction records to manage, and the operational detail behind them differs by channel.


**Settlement** timelines are a clear example. Across Xendit's


[available payment channels](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-channels) , settlement ranges from instant on channels such as PromptPay in Thailand and several Indonesian virtual accounts, through T+1 business days on BCA Virtual Account, out to T+5 business days on cards.


**Refund** behavior varies too, with some channels supporting partial refunds inside a defined validity window and others supporting none. For your finance team, that variation means knowing an order is paid tells them very little on its own, since it does not show when the money will reach your account or whether that order can still be refunded.


### **4. Payment needs change when your business adds physical channels**


An online-first brand may eventually open a flagship store, run pop-ups, or sell at events. Each of those creates a


**second payment environment to manage alongside the existing online checkout** .


Handled


**separately** , your business ends up with one provider for the website, another for in-person sales, and two sets of records that finance has to line up manually at month end. Opening a store then adds


**reconciliation work** that your team has to absorb on top of its existing workload.


These five sources of payment friction lead to the same requirement. Your payment infrastructure has to support several different customer journeys at once without adding a matching layer of internal complexity each time.


## **What e-commerce businesses need from payment infrastructure in Southeast Asia**


As payment needs spread across markets and channels, four capabilities decide whether your setup keeps up with growth or becomes the thing slowing it down.


Here are the


**payment infrastructure capabilities your e-commerce business needs** in Southeast Asia, and how


**Xendit** supports each one:

**relevant local and international payment method options** available in every market you sell in.

The local mix is specific to each market, covering QRIS and virtual accounts from BCA, BRI, and Mandiri in Indonesia, GCash and Maya in the Philippines, PromptPay in Thailand, FPX in Malaysia, MoMo and ZaloPay in Vietnam, and PayNow in Singapore.


Adding a channel is a configuration step instead of an engineering project. Your team can


[activate payment channels](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/activate-payment-channels) directly from the Xendit Dashboard, with many available immediately after account verification. For your business, that means you can respond to conversion data by turning on a method in a specific market, without waiting on a release cycle.


### **Reliable payment processing as volume grows**

With Xendit, your business processes transactions through the

Every transaction returns an ID you can track, and a webhook confirms the outcome once the customer finishes their part. Xendit maintains


**99.999% payment uptime** , so the infrastructure


**holds up consistently** during the campaign periods when your traffic concentrates.

Tokenization matters here as well and Xendit offers


**tokenized payment methods** that save a customer's credentials securely, removing repeated OTP steps for returning buyers. For your business, that removes a known drop-off point from the repeat purchase flow, where a customer who already intends to buy is asked to re-authenticate from scratch.

### **Visibility across payment operations**


More transactions also mean more refunds, settlements, and records for your teams to account for.


With Xendit, your business monitors payment activity through the


[Xendit Dashboard](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/your-dashboard) , which runs in Test Mode for integration work and Live Mode for real transactions. The

Two parts of that reporting do most of the reconciliation work for your team:


- **The Reference field** , which carries your own external ID, so your team can match a Xendit transaction to an order in your own system


- **Report delivery** , since


[reports](https://docs.xendit.co/v1/docs/transactions-report) can be exported on demand, scheduled to email or SFTP, or pulled through the report API, so the data reaches your finance systems without anyone downloading files manually


### **Licensed infrastructure across Southeast Asian markets**


Global e-commerce businesses need payment infrastructure that supports


**regional growth** without a completely different setup in every market, and enterprise procurement teams check the regulatory basis for that before anything goes live.


Xendit's infrastructure is supported by


[licensed entities across Southeast Asia](https://www.xendit.co/en-id/company/xendit-licenses-2/) , including a Payment Gateway licence from Bank Indonesia, Operator of Payment System registration from Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, Major Payment Institution status from the Monetary Authority of Singapore, Merchant Acquiring Services from Bank Negara Malaysia, Payment Service Provider licensing from the Bank of Thailand, Payment Intermediary Services from the State Bank of Vietnam, and a Money Service Operator licence in Hong Kong, with the relevant licences held by entities within the Xendit group.


For your business, this gives you a


**payment partner with local regulatory presence across multiple markets** , so your legal and risk teams review one partner instead of building and vetting separate relationships country by country.


***Also read:***[What to Look for in a Payment Partner When Expanding from the US to Southeast Asia](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/what-to-look-for-payment-partner-expanding-us-to-southeast-asia/)


These four capabilities work together in practice, and one Xendit customer shows what that combination does for a growing online brand.


## **How MASSHIRO&Co. applied these capabilities**


[MASSHIRO&Co.](https://www.xendit.co/en/case-study/masshiroco-delighting-shoppers-with-ease-of-payments/) is an Indonesian fashion brand founded in 2015 and a long-standing Xendit customer, selling its shirt collections through its own online store.


**The problem**


As the brand grew,


**orders started arriving from customers outside Indonesia** , including Singapore, Malaysia, Austria, and the Netherlands. The team could not


**process those payments** , so it had to decline the orders and cap its own growth at the border. Domestic demand presented a separate version of the same issue, since Indonesian customers wanted to pay through bank transfers and e-wallets that


**the store did not support** .


**What changed**


Working with Xendit, MASSHIRO&Co. addressed both sides of the problem through the same payment setup:


- **International**[card acceptance](https://www.xendit.co/en/payment-channel/?ordr=title&pm-category=cards) , which let the brand take orders from the foreign customers it had previously turned away


- **Domestic**[payment methods](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-channels) , including bank transfers and e-wallets such as OVO, which matched how Indonesian shoppers already preferred to pay online


- [Payment Links](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/payment-links/) , which the team generates from the Xendit Dashboard and sends through WhatsApp or Instagram when a customer prefers to shop by chat. The brand's customer service team handles manual transactions by sending a link inside the conversation, so the sale completes where it started.


MASSHIRO&Co. also planned to open a


**larger flagship store** , which would


**add in-person payments** to a setup that began as a website checkout. The takeaway for your business is that the payment infrastructure solving today's online problem should also carry the next sales channel, so adding a store becomes a configuration decision instead of a separate payment project.

## **FAQ for e-commerce businesses in Southeast Asia: Building a payment setup**


### **How many payment methods should an e-commerce business offer in each Southeast Asian market?**


Enough to cover how most customers in that market already pay, which usually means the leading e-wallets, the local bank transfer or virtual account rails, QR, and cards for international buyers. Adding methods no one uses in that country adds maintenance without adding conversion.


**Xendit** gives your business access to


[more than 100 payment methods](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/all-payment-methods/) across its supported markets through one integration, and you can


[activate channels per market](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/activate-payment-channels) from the Dashboard, so you can start with the top options and widen the mix as your own conversion data comes in.


### **Can you collect payment from customers who buy through WhatsApp or Instagram instead of your website?**


Yes. Your team can send a payment link or a scannable QR code inside the conversation, so the customer completes the purchase without being redirected to a separate site.


[Xendit Payment Links](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/payment-links/) can be created in the Dashboard, generated through the API, or sent through messaging apps such as WhatsApp and Viber, with a branded checkout page and automated reminders attached. This is the same approach


[MASSHIRO&Co.](https://www.xendit.co/en/case-study/masshiroco-delighting-shoppers-with-ease-of-payments/) uses when customers prefer to shop by chat.


### **How long does it take for e-commerce payments to settle in Southeast Asia?**


[Settlement depends on the payment channel and market](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-channels) , running from instant on channels such as PromptPay and several Indonesian virtual accounts, to T+1 business days on some bank channels, out to T+5 business days on cards.


**Xendit** also offers


[early settlement](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/all-payment-methods/) for businesses that need access to funds ahead of the standard timeline.


### **Can international customers pay on a Southeast Asia e-commerce store?**


They can, provided your checkout accepts international card payments alongside local methods. Declining foreign orders because the payment cannot be processed is a common ceiling for growing brands, which is exactly the problem


[MASSHIRO&Co.](https://www.xendit.co/en/case-study/masshiroco-delighting-shoppers-with-ease-of-payments/) faced before working with Xendit. With


**Xendit** , your business can accept international cards and


[local payment methods](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-channels) through the same integration, so overseas demand and domestic demand are handled by one setup.


### **How do you keep track of refunds and settlement across several payment methods?**


You need transaction-level records that show settlement status and refund status per payment, since these behave differently on each channel. The


[Xendit Transactions report](https://docs.xendit.co/v1/docs/transactions-report) presents each transaction on one line with its status, channel, fees, net amount, settlement status, estimated settlement date, refund status, and failure reason, and it can be exported on demand, scheduled to email or SFTP, or pulled through the report API. Your team can also match records using the Reference field, which carries your own order ID, and monitor payment activity directly in the


[Xendit Dashboard](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/your-dashboard) .


### **Can the same payment setup handle both online orders and in-store sales?**


Yes, and keeping them on one setup avoids a second reconciliation process later.


**Xendit** supports online checkout through its


[Payments API](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/payments-via-api-overview) and plug-ins, chat and link-based collection through


[Payment Links](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/payment-links/) , and in-person payments through


[POS terminals](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/pos-terminal/) that accept cards, QRIS, and e-money. Because online payments, in-person payments, and refunds are recorded as transaction types within the same


[Transactions report](https://docs.xendit.co/v1/docs/transactions-report) , your finance team reconciles all three sales channels from one export.
